lessons.title: The Rs 1.5 Lakh Limit: How Much Tax You Actually Save

children.text: "Invest ₹1.5 lakh and save ₹46,800 in tax." You have seen that line on fund house ads and insurance brochures. It is true for some people and badly wrong for most. The real number depends on two things: how much of the limit you have already used, and which slab the deduction comes out of. This lesson teaches you to calculate your own number instead of trusting the brochure.
One Combined Ceiling, Not a Limit Per Product

The ₹1,50,000 cap under Section 123 (80C) applies to the total of everything eligible in the tax year. EPF, PPF, ELSS, insurance premiums, tuition fees and home loan principal all share the same bucket. Once the bucket is full, every extra rupee you put in earns zero additional deduction.

cells: Her EPF contribution (12% of ₹50,000 basic × 12 months)

body.text: The excess is not wasted money. Anjali's extra ₹52,000 in PPF still earns tax-free interest. It simply does not reduce this year's tax. The mistake would be choosing a product only for the deduction after the limit is already full.

body.title: Limit Check
body.question: Arjun works at a PSU in Bhopal. His own EPF and VPF contributions for the year total ₹1,80,000. His father suggests he also buy an ELSS fund to 'max out 80C'. What is the maximum deduction Arjun can claim under Section 123 (80C)?
options: ₹1,80,000 plus whatever he puts into ELSS
₹1,50,000, and ELSS adds nothing to it
₹1,50,000 only if he invests in ELSS
body.explanation: His EPF and VPF alone already exceed ₹1,50,000, so his 80C bucket is full. An ELSS investment might still suit his goals, but it cannot increase his deduction by a single rupee.

children.text: Your Slab Decides What the Deduction Is Worth
A deduction knocks income off the top of your taxable income, so it saves tax at your highest (marginal) slab first. When the whole deduction sits inside one slab, the maths is simple.

body.title: Quick Check
body.textWithBlank: The same ₹1,50,000 deduction saves six times more tax for someone in the 30% slab than for someone in the ___ slab.
body.explanation: ₹46,800 at 30% divided by ₹7,800 at 5% is exactly 6. The deduction is identical; the tax saved is not.

children.text: When the Deduction Straddles Two Slabs
If your taxable income sits just above a slab boundary, part of the deduction saves tax at the higher rate and the rest at the lower rate. Split it at the boundary and calculate each piece.

body.title: Your Turn: Split the Slabs
body.prompt: Pooja, a doctor in Lucknow on the old regime, has taxable income of ₹10,60,000 before 80C. She claims the full ₹1,50,000. How much tax does she save, including 4% cess?
body.explanation: Only ₹60,000 of her income is above ₹10 lakh, so ₹60,000 × 30% = ₹18,000. The remaining ₹90,000 of the deduction comes out of the 20% slab: ₹90,000 × 20% = ₹18,000. Total ₹36,000, plus 4% cess = ₹37,440. Using 30% on the whole ₹1,50,000 would have overstated her saving by ₹9,360.

children.text: The Rebate Effect: When 80C Is Worth More Than Your Slab

The old regime gives a full rebate of up to ₹12,500 if your taxable income is ₹5,00,000 or less. If 80C pulls your taxable income below that line, your entire tax disappears, not just the slab-rate portion.

body.label: Suresh's effective saving rate
body.context: ₹37,960 saved on a ₹1,50,000 deduction, even though his top slab is only 20%. The rebate turned the last stretch of the deduction into a jackpot.

body.text: Before celebrating, check the new regime. If Suresh's taxable income of ₹6,20,000 came from a salary of ₹6,70,000 after the ₹50,000 old-regime standard deduction, the new regime would take ₹75,000 off instead, leave ₹5,95,000, and the ₹12 lakh rebate would make his tax zero with no investment at all. For most people earning under about ₹12.75 lakh in salary, 80C is not needed to reach zero tax.

body.title: Scenario: The March ELSS Rush
body.scenario: Divya is a product manager in Chennai on the old regime, with taxable income comfortably above ₹15 lakh. In the tax year she has already contributed ₹96,000 to EPF, paid ₹18,000 in term insurance premium and paid ₹60,000 in tuition fees for her daughter's school. On 25 March, a relationship manager calls to pitch a ₹1,50,000 ELSS lump sum 'to save ₹46,800 before the deadline'.
body.prompt: How much extra tax will the ELSS investment save Divya this year? What should she do instead?
body.modelAnswer: Zero. Her EPF, term premium and tuition fees add up to ₹1,74,000, which is already ₹24,000 over the ₹1,50,000 limit. The ELSS investment adds nothing to her deduction. If she likes the idea of equity exposure, she can invest based on her goals, ideally through a SIP rather than a last-minute lump sum, and with no 3-year lock-in if she chooses a regular flexi-cap or index fund. For future years, she should add up her automatic 80C items in April, not March, so she knows her real gap before anyone calls.

Go Deeper: High Earners and Surcharge

children.text: Above ₹50 lakh of income, a surcharge is added on top of your tax, and cess is charged on tax plus surcharge. That lifts the effective rate on your top rupees, so a full 80C deduction is worth a little more. The figures below assume the entire ₹1,50,000 falls within one surcharge band.

content.caption: Old regime surcharge bands and the value of a full ₹1,50,000 deduction

content.text: Near a surcharge threshold, marginal relief caps the surcharge, and a deduction that pulls income below ₹50 lakh or ₹1 crore can save more or less than these figures. Run the exact numbers in the official tax calculator or with a CA if you are close to a threshold.

body.title: Find Your Real 80C Number
steps: Pull your latest payslip and multiply your monthly employee EPF (plus any VPF) by the months left in the tax year, adding what has already been deducted
Add premiums for life insurance policies on yourself, your spouse or your children
Add tuition fees paid for up to two children and the principal part of home loan EMIs
Subtract the total from ₹1,50,000. If the answer is zero or negative, your bucket is already full.
Note your taxable income before 80C and check whether the deduction straddles a slab boundary or crosses the ₹5 lakh rebate line
Calculate your tax saved slab by slab, then compare the result against your tax under the new regime

body.label: Income Tax Department: Tax Calculator
body.description: Enter your income with and without the 80C deduction to see your exact saving, including rebate and surcharge effects.

points: ₹1,50,000 is one combined limit across all eligible items, not a limit per product.
EPF, insurance premiums, tuition fees and home loan principal often fill most of the bucket automatically.
Tax saved equals deduction × marginal slab rate × 1.04 when the deduction stays within one slab: ₹7,800, ₹31,200 or ₹46,800.
If the deduction straddles two slabs, split it at the boundary and calculate each part separately.
Crossing below ₹5 lakh taxable income triggers the old-regime rebate and can make the saving larger than your slab rate suggests.
Always compare against the new regime, which often reaches zero tax for salaries up to about ₹12.75 lakh without any 80C investment.

body.text: This lesson is for educational purposes only and is not tax, legal or investment advice. Figures use old regime slab rates, the 4% health and education cess and surcharge rates applicable at the time of writing, which can change with each Union Budget. Consult a qualified Chartered Accountant for decisions specific to your situation.
